segments.title: Chương 278: 0280 [Người phụ trách niêm yết]
segments.content:
Within a few days, Mizuki Shuhei posted thirty to forty articles on Hainei Net, all of which were old pieces he had previously published on other websites.

Chen Guiliang found some time to read a few of them.

Well, in terms of content quality, it was hard to find words.

This person's so-called "proper worldview" was to always side with the masses. It had a rather populist flavor. Later, he picked the right lane and made a living entirely off of patriotism.

Chen Guiliang saw an article he wrote during this year's Gaokao period. It began by saying there are many paths in life, and going to college is just one of them. This statement was, of course, correct.

But then he went on to say that the Gaokao was one of the poorer paths. Going to college was of no help to most professions. He also cited a survey showing that ninety percent of Chinese university students now work in careers unrelated to their majors...

Chen Guiliang seriously doubted if this person had ever attended university.

He was greatly disappointed.

But the man was quite popular with the vast number of netizens. Since his arrival, his Hainei Net account had always been bustling with activity.

During the National Day holiday.

Thanks to Huang Xinyuan pulling some strings, the ringback tone downloads for "Wait a Minute" skyrocketed with recommendations from China Mobile and China Unicom. ByteDance's profits for the latter half of the year looked promising.

Over at Game Science, they had also started recruiting a Java team to develop mobile games. Aside from one or two core members who needed to be poached from other companies, the rest were mostly students from Beijing's universities, with a prevalence of juniors and seniors from Tsinghua and Peking University.

After repeated discussions and arguments, venture capital firms like Carlyle, IDG, and GGV recommended a talent to help with the public listing.

Before this person arrived in Beijing, Chen Guiliang made a point of talking to ByteDance's CFO, Chang Zhongxiang.

The financial system of ByteDance was built single-handedly by Chang Zhongxiang. Now, he needed to be properly appeased and reassured, to prevent any internal strife during the IPO process.

This was because the person in charge of an IPO often parachutes in as the company's new CFO.

"Old Chang, you're here. Have a seat," Chen Guiliang said with a broad smile.

To be obsequious for no reason means you're either a villain or a thief.

Chang Zhongxiang felt a chill down his spine. He sat down in a daze and asked, "What is it, Boss?"

Chen Guiliang said, "Isn't the company planning to go public? The major VCs have been bickering for a month, and now they've reached an agreement. They're jointly recommending a talent to come over."

Chang Zhongxiang knew a bit about IPOs, but he had only participated in parts of them before and wasn't familiar with the entire process. He gave a wry smile, "Are you reassigning me?"

Chen Guiliang placated him, "You'll continue as CFO. When this person arrives, I will appoint him as the 'Head of IPO'. But you should also know that dual leadership causes many problems. So, until the listing is successful, he will have absolute authority, and your team must cooperate fully. If he encounters any obstruction, he can report directly to me and the board."

"I understand. No matter how I feel, I can't cause trouble at a time like this." Chang Zhongxiang let out a long sigh of relief. As long as he wasn't being replaced, it was fine. This showed that the boss still trusted and valued him.

Chang Zhongxiang held stock options and was also hoping for the company to go public soon.

ByteDance's current situation completely met the basic requirements for a US listing.

Two years ago, when KongZhong Corporation went public in the US, it only had 137 employees and had just broken even. However, its revenue was larger than ByteDance's.

Over 80% of its revenue came from Monternet, and its prospectus had a risk warning about over-reliance on a single partner. Yet, it still completed its IPO and listed successfully.

Now, Xiaonei Net and Hainei Net were leaders in their respective industries. Hainei Net's WAP site revenue was rising rapidly. Kaixin Market had been largely left alone, but it had a large and active user base and generated net profit every month.

The guy recommended by the VCs was named Lü Zhihui. He graduated from Fudan University in 1986, then went to the US for his master's and doctorate. He had worked at several investment banks and was currently at Goldman Sachs.

He had managed the entire process of a state-owned enterprise listing in the US and had also partially participated in the US listings of six Chinese IT companies.

Hiring someone like him was very expensive.

The signing bonus alone was $200,000 to compensate for his losses from leaving Goldman Sachs. His base annual salary was negotiated at $400,000, higher than that of any other executive at ByteDance.

There were also phased bonuses.

A certain amount for passing the SEC review, a certain amount for a successful listing, and another bonus if the stock price exceeded a benchmark within six months of listing.

Due to the scarcity of such talent at the time, he also had to be given a small number of restricted shares or options. If the stock price increase exceeded a certain number within a year of listing, he would be granted another small amount of equity.

The day Lü Zhihui arrived, Chen Guiliang led all the executives in a warm welcome.

They had lunch at a high-end restaurant, and during the meal, the executives gave a general overview of the company's situation.

After listening, Lü Zhihui already had a clear picture: "The top priority is to register a company overseas, in a place like the Cayman Islands. Xiaonei Net and Hainei Net must hold ICP licenses, and foreign entities are strictly prohibited from directly holding these. Also, the UGC content on both websites falls under internet publishing services, and foreign involvement requires special approval from the Ministry of Truth. Without registering an offshore company in the Cayman Islands to create a shell, ByteDance will never be able to list in the United States."

"Understood," Chen Guiliang nodded.

Sina, Sohu, and Baidu had all done it this way. Otherwise, the Chinese government wouldn't approve, and the US side would also see it as a risk.

This required setting up a VIE structure, preparing legal documents, and coordinating with law firms in both China and the US.

Next was the financial audit. Lü Zhihui was very satisfied with the internal financial control system Chang Zhongxiang had built; it could be used directly without any adjustments. This would save Lü Zhihui a lot of time and effort.

As for negotiating underwriting with investment banks, it was still too early. They needed to get the VIE structure and financial audit sorted out first.

Chen Guiliang asked, "What is the typical IPO cycle for Chinese IT companies listing in the US right now?"

Lü Zhihui said, "The fastest is 14 months, and slower ones can drag on for more than 20 months. Those that take a long time are mainly stuck in the conversion between Chinese and US accounting standards. I have experience in this area, so I definitely won't let it cause delays."

Ao Yanchen couldn't help but ask, "How much does it cost to go public?"

Lü Zhihui replied, "The current listing cost for Chinese IT companies is between 10 and 20 million US dollars. It depends on how much is raised; the cost is about 10-15% of the funds raised."

"It costs that much to go public?" Xie Yang was shocked.

Lü Zhihui knew that most executives at Chinese companies today were completely clueless about IPOs.

He explained in detail, "The company doesn't have to pay for all of it. For example, when raising funds, you need top investment banks for underwriting, and they charge an underwriting fee of 5-7%. It depends on the bank. Goldman Sachs, where I used to work, charges the most, but they also have the highest success rate."

"Then there are the audit fees for the Big Four accounting firms, totaling between 1.5 and 3 million US dollars. The more difficult the audit, the more expensive it is. If you pay enough, it's even possible to get an audit passed that otherwise wouldn't."

"There are also IPO legal fees, which have to be paid to lawyers in both China and the US. The fees are roughly between 2 and 5 million US dollars."

This was why talent for listings was so scarce. It required coordinating with law firms in both China and the US, as well as with the Big Four accounting firms. One also had to lead changes in the company's structure and financial system, and deal with the investment banks handling the fundraising...

Over the next period, Chen Guiliang convened a board meeting and also invited investors from several firms.

Everyone worked together with one heart and one mind, all for a successful listing.

Professor Wu, as ByteDance's independent director, even treated the company as his own research project. This time, he was exceptionally proactive, personally leading several of his graduate students to assist Lü Zhihui. Compensation wasn't an issue; the main thing was to be able to participate.

The graduate students were even more excited. No matter what they did in the future, and regardless of whether ByteDance listed successfully, this experience would be an asset on their resumes.

During this busy period, Chen Guiliang called over Bian Guanyue and, at the same time, finalized the property transfer with Liu Jianguo.

Liu Jianguo took them to the apartment and handed over the keys, saying, "The renovation was just finished two or three months ago. I haven't lived in it for a single day. But I have two other renovated apartments downstairs, so we'll be neighbors from now on."
